Abstract.AbstractText: Painful diabetic neuropathy (PDN) is a type of peripheral neuropathic pain that is often intractable. Elevated nitric oxide (NO) from neuronal and non-neuronal sources in the somatosensory system is implicated in the pathobiology of peripheral neuropathic pain. However, in diabetes, nitrergic nerve degeneration to deplete nitric oxide (NO) bioactivity appears causal in the pathogenesis of irreversible autonomic neuropathy, another longterm complication of diabetes. Hence, we hypothesized that progressive NO depletion may underpin the pathobiology of PDN and that NO donors may alleviate PDN. Diabetes was induced in rats with intravenous streptozotocin (STZ) at 70 mg/kg and confirmed if blood glucose levels on day 10 post-STZ were ≥ 15mM. Analgesic efficacy of subcutaneous bolus doses of the furoxan NO donor, PRG150 was assessed in the STZ-diabetic rat model of PDN at 10-, 14- and 24-wks post-STZ relative to the sydnominine NO donor, SIN-1 and its prodrug, molsidomine. PRG150 produced dose-dependent analgesia in STZ-diabetic rats whereas SIN-1 and molsidomine evoked neuro-excitatory side-effects, but not analgesia. The 1,000-fold larger doses of PRG150 needed to produce analgesia at 14- and 24-wks (800 pmol/kg) c.f. 10-wks (8 fmol/kg) post-STZ in rats, suggest that progressive NO depletion is also causal in PDN. Importantly, doses of PRG150 up to 10,000 fold higher than the analgesic dose did not produce hypotension in rats. The 50-fold greater release of NO by SIN-1 c.f. PRG150 in vitro, may underpin the neuro-excitatory rather than analgesic effects of SIN-1/molsidomine. PRG150 is worthy of further investigation as a potential novel analgesic for PDN.
